QF.id: XIII Introduction to Forwards and Futures_63

question.text: What determines whether a commodity market is in contango or backwardation?

answer.text: If storage cost plus interest cost exceeds convenience yield, the market is in contango (futures above spot). If convenience yield exceeds storage plus interest cost, the market is in backwardation (futures below spot)
Only supply and demand determine whether markets are in contango or backwardation
Commodity markets are always in contango because storage costs are always positive
Government price controls determine contango or backwardation

explanation.text: The Logic: The commodity cost-of-carry model is F = S x e^((r + s - c)t), where r is interest, s is storage cost, and c is convenience yield. When (r + s) exceeds c, futures trade above spot (contango). When c exceeds (r + s), futures trade below spot (backwardation). A high convenience yield from tight physical supply drives backwardation, while ample supply with low convenience yield supports contango. The Trap: Supply and demand influence convenience yield, but the formal relationship involves all three carry components. Pure storage markets with no convenience yield tend to be in contango, not always. Government price controls are not the structural driver of contango or backwardation. Note: Replaced the truncated "F < S" expression with explicit "futures below spot/backwardation" wording so the second condition is now complete; distributor/cross-exam framing removed.
